myth: The root bridges are natural, and grew across the rivers by themselves.

They are made by people. Families spend years training the roots, tying, twisting and weaving them, and keep repairing the bridges over generations. Without that care, the roots would just hang or spread into the forest.

sec.t:
The most famous root bridge is near the village of Nongriat, a steep walk of a few thousand steps down from the nearest road. It has two levels, one above the other, both made of living roots. Visitors climb down to see it, and to swim in the blue pools below.

Researchers have counted dozens of these bridges across the Khasi and Jaintia hills, from short spans to ones longer than a cricket pitch. Some villages grow ladders, platforms and even viewing towers from roots too. In 2022, India put the root bridges on UNESCO's tentative list, the first step towards becoming a World Heritage Site.

Building a root bridge takes patience. It often takes 15 years or more before a new bridge is strong enough to cross, and many keep strengthening for long after. Older people start bridges that their grandchildren will use.

Engineers and architects from other countries have studied them. They are interested in how roots fuse together where they touch, making a strong mesh, and in how a living structure repairs itself. Some think the same ideas could one day help design greener structures in cities. The rubber fig is a cousin of the [[@banyan|banyan]], another tree famous for its aerial roots.

The root bridges are only one part of Meghalaya's story. Its limestone hills hide some of the longest [[@caves-form|caves]] in India, carved out by rainwater over millions of years. Krem Liat Prah, one of the longest known, has passages running for more than 30 km.

The Khasi, Jaintia and Garo communities have their own languages and customs. In Khasi families, children usually take their mother's clan name. Mawlynnong, a small village near the Bangladesh border, became famous after a travel magazine called it Asia's cleanest village in 2003. Paths are swept daily and bamboo dustbins stand by the road. Above it all, the clouds roll in, as they have for as long as anyone remembers.

text: Long ago, Mumbai was seven low islands off the Konkan coast: Colaba, Old Woman's Island, Bombay Island, Mazagaon, Parel, Worli and Mahim. Koli fishing families lived there, sailing out from small villages. At high tide the sea flooded the gaps between the islands. At low tide some of them could almost be crossed on foot.

From the 1700s, the British began building sea walls and filling in the shallow water. Over about 150 years the islands joined into one long strip of land. Today a city of more than 2 crore people, counting its suburbs, sits on that land.

st.prompt: How were Mumbai's seven islands joined into one?

options.t: People filled the sea between them with rock and earth
Sand from the monsoon slowly piled up between them

st.reveal: Starting in the 1700s, the British built walls and causeways and filled shallow creeks with rock and soil. This is called land reclamation. Over about 150 years the islands merged into one long piece of land.

myth: Mumbai is the capital of India.
India's capital is New Delhi. Mumbai is the capital of the state of Maharashtra and India's biggest centre of business and banking, which is why people sometimes call it the financial capital.

sec.t:
Portugal took the islands in 1534. In 1661, King Charles II of England married the Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza, and the islands were part of her dowry. The king had little use for them. In 1668 he rented them to the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] for £10 a year.

The Company saw what the king had missed: a deep, sheltered harbour, perfect for big ships. Merchants, shipbuilders and workers arrived from Gujarat, the Konkan and much further away.

The biggest early project was the Hornby Vellard, a sea wall finished in the 1780s. It stopped the tide flooding the low land around Worli, so it could be drained and built on. More causeways and fillings followed. Hills were cut down and the rock and soil dumped into creeks.

By the late 1800s the seven islands were one. Work never fully stopped. Areas such as Nariman Point and Cuffe Parade were built on reclaimed land in the 1900s. Along the edges, [[@mangroves|mangrove]] forests still grow in the salty mud, as they did before the city came.

On 16 April 1853 the first passenger train in India ran from Bombay to Thane, about 34 km. The [[@indian-railways|railways]] and the port turned the city into a giant trading hub. [[@clothes-cotton|Cotton]] mills grew up in Parel and attracted thousands of workers. The grand railway station now called Chhatrapati [[@shivaji|Shivaji]] Terminus, finished in 1888, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Today Mumbai's [[@india-wonder-mumbai-local|suburban trains]] carry about 75 lakh people a day. A train every few minutes moves office workers, schoolchildren and even home-cooked lunches.

{{story:lunchbox-dabbawala}}

The city is also home to Hindi cinema, often called [[@bollywood|Bollywood]], which makes hundreds of films a year.

Mumbai's people come from every corner of India, and its calendar shows it. During [[@ganesh-chaturthi|Ganesh Chaturthi]], huge idols of [[@myths-ganesha-stories|Ganesha]] are carried through the streets to the sea, with drums and crowds that fill whole roads. Eid, Christmas, Diwali and the Parsi New Year are all celebrated in the city. The Parsis, whose ancestors came from [[@ancient-persia|Persia]], helped build much of old Bombay's industry, shipyards and schools.

Because so much of Mumbai is low, filled-in land, heavy rain can flood it fast. On 26 July 2005, nearly a metre of rain fell on parts of the city in a single day. Since then, drains and pumping stations have been improved, but every [[@monsoon|monsoon]] still tests the city.

The name Mumbai comes from Mumbadevi, a goddess worshipped by the Kolis. The Portuguese and British called the place Bombay, and some say that name came from Portuguese words for "good bay". In 1995 the city's name was officially changed to Mumbai, the name [[@marathi-gujarati|Marathi]] and Gujarati speakers had always used.

text: South Korea is a country on the southern half of the Korean Peninsula in East Asia, between China and Japan. It has about 5.2 crore people, and around half of them live in and around the capital, Seoul. The country is mountainous, with hot, wet summers and freezing winters.

Its story is one of the fastest turnarounds in history. After the Korean War ended in 1953, it was among the poorest countries in the world. Today it builds smartphones, cars and huge ships, has some of the fastest internet anywhere, and sends [[@kpop|K-pop]] songs, films and dramas around the planet. Old palaces, Buddhist temples and kimchi pots sit right next to glass towers.

st.prompt: King Sejong created the Korean alphabet, Hangul, in the 1440s. How long did he say a clever person would take to learn it?
st.reveal: An old book that explains the script says a wise person can learn it before a morning is over, and even a slow learner within ten days. Hangul has only 24 basic letters today, and their shapes are based on the shape of the mouth and tongue making each sound.

This "fan death" idea was once widely believed in South Korea, and some fans were even sold with timers for safety. There is no scientific evidence that a fan can kill a healthy person this way.

sec.t:
Korea was a single kingdom for centuries. Japan ruled it from 1910 to 1945. After the Second World War, the peninsula was split between areas occupied by the Soviet Union in the north and the USA in the south. In 1950 the North invaded the South, and the Korean War drew in armies from many countries, part of the [[@cold-war|Cold War]].

The fighting stopped in 1953 with an armistice, an agreement to stop fighting, but no peace treaty was ever signed. A strip of land about 4 kilometres wide, the Demilitarised Zone or DMZ, still divides the two Koreas. With few people inside it for 70 years, it has become a refuge for cranes and other wildlife. Seoul is only about 50 kilometres from that border.

sec.h: An alphabet made by a king

sec.t:
Kimchi, spicy fermented cabbage with radish, garlic and chilli, appears at almost every meal. In late autumn, families and neighbours gather to make huge batches together, a tradition called kimjang that UNESCO lists as part of humanity's cultural heritage. The vegetables slowly [[@fermentation|ferment]] through the winter, turning sour and tangy, a little like an Indian [[@pickles-achar|achar]].

Korean homes have long been heated from below. In the old ondol system, smoke from a kitchen fire ran through channels under a stone floor. Modern homes use hot water pipes instead, which is why many Koreans sit, eat and even sleep on the warm floor.

In the middle of Seoul there was once a stream called Cheonggyecheon. As the city grew, it was covered with concrete and an elevated motorway was built on top. In 2003 the city tore down the motorway and dug the stream back out. It reopened in 2005 as a green walkway about 11 kilometres long, cooler than the streets around it. [[@urban-planning|City planners]] from many countries have visited to see how a road could be swapped for a river.

text: The Bible is the holy book of Christianity, the world's largest religion. Its first and longer part, often called the Old Testament, is also sacred to Jews, who call it the Tanakh or Hebrew Bible. The second part, the New Testament, is about the life and teachings of Jesus and his early followers.

It isn't one book written in one go. It is a library of dozens of books: laws, histories, poems, songs, wise sayings, prophecies and letters. Most were written in Hebrew or Greek, with some passages in Aramaic. Christians around the world read it in prayer and worship, and many believe it carries the word of God.

st.prompt: The word "Bible" comes from an ancient Greek word. What did that word mean?
st.reveal: Greek biblia means "books", or "little books". It came from Byblos, a port in today's Lebanon that traded papyrus, the paper of the ancient world. The name fits, since the Bible is a collection of many books.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bible.

Library of Congress, the Gutenberg Bible.
n.certNote: Christians and Jews hold the Bible to be sacred, and many believe it is inspired by God. Historians and religious scholars hold a range of views on who wrote each book and when, and these questions are still debated.

It is a collection of many writings, including history, laws, poems, songs, stories and letters. Many different writers produced them over a long period, and they were gathered together much later.

sec.t:
The Old Testament tells of the creation of the world, of Noah and the flood, and of Abraham, whom Jews, Christians and Muslims all honour. It follows Moses leading the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, and young David defeating the giant Goliath. It includes the Psalms, a book of 150 poems and songs, and the words of prophets such as Isaiah.

The New Testament begins with four Gospels, each telling the story of Jesus in its own way. Then come the Acts of the Apostles and letters written to early Christian groups, many by a traveller and teacher named Paul. It ends with Revelation, a book of visions.

Different churches include slightly different books. Most Protestant Bibles have 66, Catholic Bibles have 73 and some Orthodox Bibles have a few more.

In 1947, Bedouin shepherds exploring caves at Qumran, near the [[@dead-sea|Dead Sea]], found clay jars holding ancient scrolls. Over the next years, searchers found fragments of hundreds of manuscripts. Some had lain hidden for more than 2,000 years.

These Dead Sea Scrolls include the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible. A long scroll of Isaiah is almost complete. Scholars were struck by how closely it matches copies made about a thousand years later, showing how carefully scribes worked. Many fragments are now kept in [[@jerusalem|Jerusalem]], in a museum building whose white roof is shaped like the lid of one of the jars. Thousands of pieces have been photographed in high detail and can be viewed online by anyone.

Christians in Kerala have a tradition that Thomas, one of Jesus's twelve apostles, arrived there in 52 CE. Historians can't confirm this, but Christianity has certainly been in India for well over 1,500 years.

In 1714, a German missionary, Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg, printed the New Testament in Tamil at Tranquebar, one of the earliest Bible translations printed in an Indian language. Later, William Carey and his team at Serampore near Kolkata worked on translations into Bengali and many other languages.

The Bible has been [[@translation|translated]] more than almost any other book. By 2024, the full Bible existed in more than 700 languages, and parts of it in thousands more. In India, there are complete Bibles in Hindi, Tamil, Malayalam, Mizo, Khasi and dozens of other languages.

text: The Norse myths are the stories of the gods worshipped by the peoples of Scandinavia, the lands now called [[@norway-fjords|Norway]], Sweden and Denmark, and later Iceland. These were the people we often call [[@vikings|Vikings]]. Their gods included Odin the wise, Thor the thunderer, and Loki the shape-changing trickster.

The myths tell how the world was made from [[@myths-giants|the body of a giant]], and how the gods fought giants and monsters. They also tell how it would all end, in a great battle called Ragnarok. Most of the stories survive because a few Icelandic writers recorded them about 800 years ago.

st.prompt: Which day of the week is named after Thor?
st.reveal: Thursday is "Thor's day". Wednesday comes from Woden, the English name for Odin, and Tuesday from Tyr, a god of war. Saturday is the odd one out, named after the Roman god Saturn.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Germanic religion and mythology.
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (about 1220).

myth: Vikings wore helmets with horns on them.
No Viking-age helmet with horns has ever been found. The horned look became popular in the 1800s, partly through costumes for Richard Wagner's operas based on Germanic myths.

the Poetic Edda and the Prose Edda

sec.t:
Odin was the chief god, a wanderer who gave up one of his eyes to drink from a well of wisdom. Two ravens, Huginn and Muninn, whose names mean "thought" and "memory", flew round the world each day and told him what they saw.

Thor, Odin's son, was strong and short-tempered. With his hammer, Mjolnir, he protected gods and humans from giants. People wore small hammer-shaped charms, and archaeologists have found many of them. Freya was a goddess of love, gold and magic who rode in a chariot pulled by cats.

Loki is the hardest to pin down. Sometimes he helps the gods out of trouble with his cleverness. Sometimes he causes the trouble, and in the end he fights against them.

The Norse did write, using letters called runes, but runes were mostly carved as short messages on stone, wood or bone. The long stories were passed on by poets who learned them by heart.

After Scandinavia and [[@iceland|Iceland]] became Christian, around the year 1000, the old poems could easily have been forgotten. In about 1220, an Icelandic chieftain and scholar called Snorri Sturluson wrote the Prose Edda, partly as a guide for young poets who needed to understand the old stories. A collection of older poems, now called the Poetic Edda, survives in a manuscript from the late 1200s. Most of what we know about Norse myths comes from these two works.

sec.h: Thor, Odin and the end of the world
sec.t:
The myths end with Ragnarok, the "fate of the gods". Winter lasts three years, monsters break free, and Thor and the great serpent of the sea kill each other. Then a new green world rises from the water, and a few gods and two humans survive to begin again.

The stories have travelled far. Just as the planets carry Roman names from the [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]], English weekdays carry Norse ones. Thor became a Marvel comic hero in 1962 and later a film star, part of the long story of [[@superheroes-history|superheroes]]. The comic Thor has blond hair, but the Thor of the old poems was usually described with a red beard.
